rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God most naturally addresses the two angels assigned as driver and witness.
rows.anchor: وظاهر سياق الآيات أن المخاطب به هما الملكان الموكلان السائق والشهيد

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some instead take the addressees to be two angels among Hell's guardians.
rows.anchor: واحتمل بعضهم أن يكون الخطاب إلى ملكين من ملائكة النار وخزنتها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expanded description of the polytheist instead of a concise label marks shirk as the gravest sin and source of the listed vices.
rows.anchor: العدول في ذكر صفة الشرك عن الإيجاز إلى الإطناب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeating the order to cast him into severe punishment reinforces the earlier command and signals shirk's gravity.
rows.anchor: فألقياه في العذاب الشديد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companion is certainly the human's devil, who stays with him and whispers misguidance.
rows.anchor: وقد تكرر في كلامه تعالى ذكر القرين من الشيطان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The devil calls God “our Lord,” including himself and the human because they are disputing together.
rows.anchor: أضاف الرب إلى نفسه والإنسان الذي هو قرينه لأنهما في مقام الاختصام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The devil denies having compelled the human to transgress.
rows.anchor: أي ما أجبرته على الطغيان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The human was ready to accept the devil's whisper and chose to accept it, so the devil denies responsibility for the transgression.
rows.anchor: متهيئا مستعدا لقبول ما ألقيته إليه تلقاه باختياره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dispute between wrongdoers and their companions was treated earlier in the account of their gathering.
rows.anchor: وقد تقدم في سورة الصافات تفصيل اختصام الظالمين وأزواجهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's singular address gathers all tyrannical polytheists and their companions into one speech that applies separately to each pair.
rows.anchor: وكأنه خطاب واحد لعامة المشركين الطاغين وقرنائهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning clause is circumstantial with “do not dispute”; “the warning” is the object of “presented,” and the preposition marks means.
rows.anchor: حال من فاعل { لا تختصموا } و { بالوعيد } مفعول { قدمت } والباء للوصلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their dispute cannot help after God has conveyed His threat to those who associate others with Him and do wrong.
rows.anchor: لا نفع لكم فيه بعد ما أبلغتكم وعيدي لمن أشرك وظلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: Jabir reports the Prophet describing a person's decreed provision, deeds, lifespan, and fate; angels guard and record him, question him in the grave, and at resurrection a driver and witness accompany him. The Prophet urges seeking God's help for the grave matter ahead.
rows.anchor: عن جابر بن عبد الله قال سمعت رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم يقول

rows.speaker: تفسير القمي
rows.claim: Al-Qummi says God promised to fill Hell, then asks whether it is full; its question means there is no more room.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير القمي في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qummi's explanation depends on reading the question as a rhetorical denial.
rows.anchor: بناؤه على كون الاستفهام إنكاريا

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: Anas reports the Prophet saying Hell keeps receiving people until God places His foot in it and it contracts, while God creates more people to fill Paradise's remaining space.
rows.anchor: عن أنس قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage identifies those who will receive the certain punishment and describes their state; the God-fearing description is incidental and strengthens the warning.
rows.anchor: تذكر الآيات من يقع عليهم هذا العذاب الذي لا ريب في تحققه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given the preceding proof that punishment will occur, the punished are necessarily deniers; the verse directly attaches woe to them.
rows.anchor: الجملة تدل على كون المعذبين هم المكذبين بالاستلزام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, since certain punishment falls only on those who disbelieve God and deny the Resurrection, woe therefore falls on them.
rows.anchor: أو التقدير إذا كان العذاب واقعا لا محالة

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines khawd literally as entering and passing through water, then metaphorically as engaging in matters; Qur'anic usage is mostly blameworthy.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب الخوض هو الشروع في الماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The indefinite form of “engagement” implies an omitted quality, understood as “remarkable.”
rows.anchor: وتنوين التنكير في { خوض } يدل على صفة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Play is activity with only an imagined effect; their futile disputation about and mockery of God's signs is therefore called play.
rows.anchor: واللعب من الأفعال ما ليس له إلا الأثر الخيالي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verb for driving means to push forcefully, and the day phrase explains “that day” in the preceding verse.
rows.anchor: الدع هو الدفع الشديد، والظاهر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They are told this is the fire whose existence and punishment of sinners the prophets conveyed by revelation, and which they denied.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالتكذيب بالنار التكذيب بما أخبر به الأنبياء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The fire now before them is the reality of what the prophets foretold.
rows.anchor: هذه مصداق ما أخبر به الأنبياء فكذبتم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question rebukes them: the plainly visible fire is neither magic, as they called prophetic warnings, nor an imaginary fable.
rows.anchor: والاستفهام للإنكار تفريعا لهم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: Zadhan transmits from Ali that the Prophet said believers and their children are in Paradise, then recited this verse.
rows.anchor: في المجمع روى زاذان عن علي عليه السلام قال قال رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports the Prophet saying God raises a believer's offspring to the believer's rank despite their lesser deeds, without reducing the parents' reward.
rows.anchor: أخرج البزار وابن مردويه عن ابن عباس رفعه إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قال

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn Abbas reports a man in Paradise asking about his parents and children; after learning they fell short of his rank, he asks God to join them to him and recites the verse.
rows.anchor: عن ابن عباس أن النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم قال إذا دخل الرجل الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse does not include the parents mentioned in that report; the clearer support for joining parents is the angels' prayer.
rows.anchor: أقول والآية لا تشمل الآباء المذكورين في الحديث

rows.speaker: تفسير القمي
rows.claim: Al-Qummi explains that Paradise has no singing or obscenity, and believers may drink without sinning.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير القمي قوله { لا لغو فيها ولا تأثيم } قال

rows.speaker: تفسير القمي
rows.claim: Al-Qummi locates the mutual questioning in Paradise.
rows.anchor: وفي تفسير القمي قوله { لا لغو فيها ولا تأثيم } قال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura treats God's unity in lordship, Resurrection, and prophethood: it affirms revelation, rejects partners, describes God's governance of creation, and ends by pointing to return and commanding worship.
rows.anchor: تذكير الأصول الثلاثة وحدانيته تعالى في ربوبيته والمعاد والنبوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sura is Meccan, as its context shows; al-Tabatabai rejects claims that some or all of it is Medinan.
rows.anchor: والسورة مكية بشهادة سياق آياتها ولا يصغى إلى قول بعضهم

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Some say this was the first sura the Prophet publicly recited to believers and polytheists together.
rows.anchor: وقد قيل إنها أول سورة أعلن النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai singles out the statement that the final destination is to the Lord as an outstanding verse.
rows.anchor: ومن غرر الآيات فيها قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He also singles out the statement that a person has only what he strives for as an outstanding verse.
rows.anchor: وقوله { وأن ليس للإنسان إلا ما سعى }

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–18 form the first of three sections, affirming revelation to the Prophet and describing him.
rows.anchor: وهي الآيات اللاتي تصدق الوحي إلى النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم وتصفه

rows.speaker: أئمة أهل البيت عليهم السلام
rows.claim: Numerous reports from the Imams say these verses describe the face-to-face revelation God gave the Prophet on the Night Journey, rather than every kind of revelation.
rows.anchor: روايات مستفيضة عن أئمة أهل البيت عليهم السلام ناصة على أن المراد بالآيات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent sense supports the Mi'raj reports; reports from Ibn Abbas, Anas, and Abu Sa'id also support this reading, which commentators generally follow while disputing details.
rows.anchor: وظاهر الآيات لا يخلو من تأييد لهذه الروايات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The apparent meaning of “star” is any luminous celestial body; its setting is its descent below the horizon.
rows.anchor: ظاهر الآية أن المراد بالنجم هو مطلق الجرم السماوي المضيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: On the preferred reading, the star's falling is its setting.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا فالمراد بهوي النجم سقوطه للغروب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One view takes the star to be the Qur'an, revealed in successive portions; al-Tabatabai says the wording does not support it.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بالنجم القرآن لنزوله نجوما

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Other reported identifications are the Pleiades and Sirius; al-Tabatabai says the wording does not support them.
rows.anchor: وقيل الثريا، وقيل الشعرى، وقيل الشهاب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view identifies the star as the shooting star cast at jinn, which Arabs call a star; the wording does not support it.
rows.anchor: وقيل الشهاب الذي يرمى به شياطين الجن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Deviation is departure from the straight path; ghayy contrasts with right guidance and attaining what is true.
rows.anchor: الضلال الخروج والانحراف عن الصراط المستقيم

rows.speaker: الراغب
rows.claim: Al-Raghib defines ghayy as ignorance based on a false belief, unlike ignorance where a person holds neither a sound nor false belief.
rows.anchor: قال الراغب الغي جهل من اعتقاد فاسد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Your companion” refers to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالصاحب هو النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet neither missed the human destination of happiness—servitude to God—nor the path leading to it, in belief or judgment.
rows.anchor: أنه لم يخطئ لا في الغاية المطلوبة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Whim” means the soul's desire and its own opinion.
rows.anchor: المراد بالهوى هوى النفس ورأيها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the negation is phrased broadly, context answers the polytheists' charge that the Prophet fabricated his call and Qur'an: in these matters he speaks from revelation, not personal desire.
rows.anchor: كان خطابا للمشركين وهم يرمونه في دعوته

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun may refer to the Prophet, the Qur'an as revelation, or revelation generally; the second object of “taught” is omitted in each construction.
rows.anchor: للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم أو للقرآن بما هو وحي

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Commentators identify the one of mighty powers as Gabriel, whom God also describes as powerful.
rows.anchor: والمراد بشديد القوى - على ما قالوا - جبريل

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reported interpretation identifies the one of mighty powers as God.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد به هو الله سبحانه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mirra can mean strength, soundness of intellect and judgment, or a kind of passing, derived from passing by.
rows.anchor: المرة بكسر الميم الشدة، وحصافة

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: If Gabriel is meant, the phrase may describe his strength before God, sound judgment, or a kind of visitation to the Prophet in the air.
rows.anchor: جبريل ذو شدة في جنب الله

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another view makes the Prophet the referent: he is strong before God, sound in judgment, or has a kind of ascent through the heavens.
rows.anchor: المراد بذو مرة النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Istawā can mean becoming upright or gaining mastery.
rows.anchor: فاستوى } بمعنى استقام أو استولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If Gabriel is the subject, he became upright in his original created form; reports say he usually appeared in different forms and appeared in his original form only twice.
rows.anchor: فاستقام جبريل على صورته الأصلية التي خلق عليها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, with Gabriel as subject, “he became established” means Gabriel mastered by his power the task entrusted to him.
rows.anchor: فاستولى جبريل بقوته على ما جعل له من الأمر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If the subject is the Prophet, the phrase means that he stood upright and became settled.
rows.anchor: وإن كان الضمير للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم فالمعنى فاستقام واستقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ufuq means a side or region.
rows.anchor: الأفق الناحية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: A reported view takes the upper horizon as the eastern side of the sky because the eastern horizon is higher than the western one on the ground; al-Tabatabai dismisses this.
rows.anchor: قيل المراد بالأفق الأعلى ناحية الشرق من السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The upper horizon is simply a higher horizon in the sky, without specifying east; “he” may be Gabriel or the Prophet, and the clause is circumstantial to “became upright.”
rows.anchor: والظاهر أن المراد به أفق أعلى من السماء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Dunū means nearness; tadallī means hanging onto something and figuratively denotes extreme closeness, with another derivation connecting it to a lowered bucket.
rows.anchor: الدنو القرب، والتدلي التعلق بالشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If both pronouns refer to Gabriel, he came close and attached himself to the Prophet to take him up to the heavens.
rows.anchor: ثم قرب جبريل فتعلق بالنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another reading with Gabriel as subject has him descend from the upper horizon, then approach the Prophet to take him to heaven.
rows.anchor: ثم تدلى جبريل من الأفق الأعلى فدنا من النبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If both pronouns refer to the Prophet, he drew near to God and increased in closeness.
rows.anchor: ثم قرب النبي من الله سبحانه وزاد في القرب

rows.speaker: المجمع
rows.claim: Al-Majmaʿ says qāb, qayb, qād, and qayd all denote an amount or measure.
rows.anchor: قال في المجمع القاب والقيب والقاد والقيد عبارة عن مقدار الشيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The bow is the familiar shooting instrument; in Hijazi usage it is also said to mean a forearm's length.
rows.anchor: القوس معروفة وهي آلة الرمي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The distance means two bows, two forearms, or closer.
rows.anchor: فكان البعد قدر قوسين أو قدر ذراعين أو أقرب

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some take qāb to mean the space between the bow's grip and tip, requiring inversion to read “the measure of two bows.”
rows.anchor: وقيل القاب ما بين مقبض القوس وسيتها ففي الكلام قلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The proposed inversion is unnecessary, since qābay qaws and qāb qawsayn mean the same thing.
rows.anchor: واعترض عليه بأن قابي قوس وقاب قوسين واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If earlier pronouns refer to Gabriel, both occurrences of “revealed” may refer to Gabriel, who revealed to God's servant, the Prophet, what he revealed.
rows.anchor: ضمير أوحى في الموضعين لجبريل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A reading allows the reference to God without prior mention because God is self-evident.
rows.anchor: ولا ضير في رجوع الضمير إليه تعالى من عدم سبق الذكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, all three pronouns refer to God, who revealed through Gabriel to His servant.
rows.anchor: الضمائر الثلاث لله والمعنى فأوحى الله بتوسط جبريل إلى عبده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another construction has the first pronoun refer to Gabriel and the second and third to God: Gabriel conveyed what God revealed to him.
rows.anchor: الضمير الأول لجبريل والثاني والثالث لله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If earlier pronouns refer to the Prophet, all three here refer to God; this is more natural than the prior reading, though that is valid.
rows.anchor: وهذا المعنى أقرب إلى الذهن من المعنى السابق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kadhb can mean spoken falsehood or error in a faculty of perception, as when one says the eye deceived someone.
rows.anchor: والكذب كما يطلق على القول والحديث الذي يلفظه اللسان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Whether kadhaba is intransitive (“the heart did not err in what it saw”) or takes two objects (“the heart did not falsely tell the Prophet what it saw”), the heart's vision was true.
rows.anchor: ما كذب الفؤاد فيما رأى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart is the Prophet's heart; the subject of “what it saw” is the heart, and the seeing is its own.
rows.anchor: وعلى هذا فالمراد بالفؤاد فؤاد النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Heart-seeing is direct self-awareness beyond senses, imagination, or thought: we witness our own sensory and mental acts through the self called the heart.
rows.anchor: فإنا كما نشاهد مدركات كل واحدة من هذه القوى بنفس تلك القوة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage does not say the object seen was God; it names the upper horizon, nearness, and revelation, while the later verse calls what was seen God's great signs.
rows.anchor: بل المرئي هو الأفق الأعلى والدنو والتدلي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Describing the vision as seeing God's great signs supports the reading that the object was the signs already mentioned.
rows.anchor: لقد رأى من آيات ربه الكبرى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Even if the verse meant that the Prophet saw God, it would be heart-sight, unlike sensory eye-sight of bodies, and could relate to God.
rows.anchor: فإنها رؤية القلب ورؤية القلب غير رؤية البصر الحسية

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: One interpretation makes the pronoun in “what he saw” refer to the Prophet: his heart did not tell his eye that it failed to recognize what it saw.
rows.anchor: وما قيل إن ضمير { ما رأى } للنبي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Another formulation says the heart did not deny the eye's vision but affirmed it; a reading with a doubled dhāl is cited in support.
rows.anchor: أن فؤاده لم يكذب بصره فيما رآه بل صدقه

rows.speaker: قارئ
rows.claim: A reader recites kadhdhaba with a doubled dhāl, supporting the interpretation that the heart affirmed what the eye saw.
rows.anchor: ويؤيده قراءة من قرأ { ما كذب } بتشديد الذال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai rejects those readings as contextually weak: God affirms the Prophet's truth in revelation and sight of the great signs; returning “he saw” to the heart preserves the argument.
rows.anchor: الذي يعطيه سياق الآيات تأييده تعالى صدق النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next question does not prove the Prophet's truth from sight; it rebukes them for disputing direct witnessing, which cannot sensibly be challenged like theoretical opinions.
rows.anchor: مسوقا للاحتجاج برؤيته على صدقه بل توبيخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The interrogative rebukes the polytheists; the pronoun denotes the Prophet, and mumārah is persistent disputation.
rows.anchor: الاستفهام للتوبيخ والخطاب للمشركين والضمير للنبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They persist in arguing with the Prophet and demanding that he accept the opposite of what he reports while seeing it directly.
rows.anchor: أفتصرون في جدالكم على النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nazla is a noun of occurrence meaning one descent; the verse describes a sighting during a different descent from the preceding one.
rows.anchor: النزلة بناء مرة من النزول فمعناه نزول واحد

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: The reported reading takes the subject as the Prophet and the object as Gabriel; the second descent is Gabriel's descent to take him to heaven.
rows.anchor: ضمير الفاعل المستكن في قوله { رآه } للنبي

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: On that reading, “at the Lote Tree” modifies the seeing, not the descent, and Gabriel is seen in his original form there.
rows.anchor: ظرف للرؤية لا للنزلة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai instead takes the object pronoun as God and the vision as heart-sight: during his ascent the Prophet descended at the Lote Tree and saw God with his heart, as at the first descent.
rows.anchor: صحة إرجاع ضمير المفعول إليه تعالى والمراد بالرؤية رؤية القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Sidr is a known tree, tāʾ marks a single tree, and muntahā appears to name a place, likely the end of the heavens because the Garden is beside it.
rows.anchor: السدر شجر معروف والتاء للوحدة والمنتهى - كأنه - اسم مكان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God does not explain what the tree is; its deliberate obscurity is reinforced by the next phrase saying only that something covers it.
rows.anchor: ولا يوجد في كلامه تعالى ما يفسر هذه الشجرة

rows.speaker: الروايات
rows.claim: Reports describe the tree as above the seventh heaven, where the deeds of Adam's descendants terminate.
rows.anchor: شجرة فوق السماء السابعة إليها تنتهي أعمال بني آدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Garden of Refuge is the final garden where believers dwell, not the provisional barzakh garden, which lasts only until resurrection.
rows.anchor: أي الجنة التي يأوي إليها المؤمنون وهي جنة الآخرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final Paradise is where believers take refuge, as the cited verses call it the Garden of Refuge and Paradise the final abode.
rows.anchor: فلهم جنات المأوى نزلا بما كانوا يعملون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Paradise is in heaven, as indicated by the statement that provision and what is promised are there.
rows.anchor: وهي في السماء على ما يدل عليه قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: قيل
rows.claim: Some identify the Garden of Refuge as the Garden of the barzakh; al-Tabatabai prefers the final Paradise.
rows.anchor: وقيل المراد بها جنة البرزخ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: To cover a thing means to surround it; mā is relative, so the phrase means whatever surrounds the tree surrounds it.
rows.anchor: غشيان الشيء الإحاطة به، و { ما } موصوله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God leaves unspecified what surrounds the tree, continuing the deliberate ambiguity about it.
rows.anchor: وقد أبهم تعالى هذا الذي يغشى السدرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Zaygh is deviation from uprightness and, for sight, inaccurate perception; tughyān is exceeding a limit and, for sight, perceiving what is unreal.
rows.anchor: الزيغ الميل عن الاستقامة، والطغيان تجاوز الحد في العمل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sight in this verse is the Prophet's.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالبصر بصر النبي صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet neither saw the object inaccurately nor saw anything unreal; he perceived without error.
rows.anchor: لم يبصر ما أبصره على غير صفته الحقيقية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This seeing is the Prophet's heart-vision, the same kind of vision as the sighting at the other descent.
rows.anchor: والمراد بالإبصار رؤيته صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بقلبه لا بجارحة العين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Min is partitive: the Prophet witnessed some of his Lord's greatest signs.
rows.anchor: للتبعيض، والمعنى أقسم لقد شاهد بعض الآيات الكبرى لربه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet completed heart-witness of God by seeing His signs, since a sign as sign points only to its source; direct sight of God's essence without sign or veil is impossible.
rows.anchor: فإن مشاهدته تعالى بالقلب إنما هي بمشاهدة آياته

rows.speaker: تفسير القمي
rows.claim: Al-Qummi gives an inward reading: the star is the Prophet, and its setting relates to his Night Journey and descent.
rows.anchor: قال النجم رسول الله صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم

rows.speaker: الرضا عليه السلام
rows.claim: Al-Tabatabai says the identification of the Prophet as the star is transmitted through al-Qummi's chain from Imam al-Rida and is an inward interpretation.
rows.anchor: وروى تسميته صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم بالنجم بإسناده عن أبيه

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر عليه السلام
rows.claim: Asked about God's oaths by the night and star, Abu Ja'far says God may swear by any creation, while creatures may swear only by God; al-Faqih gives a similar report from Abu Ja'far II.
rows.anchor: عن محمد بن مسلم قال قلت لأبي جعفر عليه السلام

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر الثاني
rows.claim: Al-Faqih transmits the same ruling on divine oaths from Ali ibn Mahziyar through Abu Ja'far II.
rows.anchor: وفي الفقيه عن علي بن مهزيار عن أبي جعفر الثاني

rows.speaker: جعفر الصادق
rows.claim: A report from Ja'far al-Sadiq says the Prophet descended from the seventh heaven on the Mi'raj night; after Utba ibn Abi Lahab heard of it, he divorced the Prophet's daughter, spat at the Prophet, and rejected the star and its Lord. The Prophet prayed for a beast to be sent against him; a lion later seized him among companions in Syria.
rows.anchor: وروت العامة عن جعفر الصادق أنه قال إن محمدا صلى الله عليه وآله وسلم
